In [[numerical analysis]], the '''uniform theory of diffraction''' ('''UTD''') is a [[high frequency|high-frequency]] method for solving [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic]] [[scattering]] problems from electrically small discontinuities or discontinuities in more than one dimension at the same point.<ref name="utd">[[Robert Kouyoumjian|R. G. Kouyoumjian]] and P. H. Pathak, "A uniform geometrical theory of diffraction for an edge in a perfectly conducting surface," ''Proc. IEEE'', vol. 62, pp. 1448–1461, November 1974. </ref> UTD is an extension of [[Joseph Keller]]'s '''geometrical theory of diffraction''' (GTD)<ref> J. B. Keller, [http://www.opticsinfobase.org/abstract.cfm?URI=josa-52-2-116 "Geometrical theory of diffraction"], ''J. Opt. Soc. Am.'', vol. 52, no. 2, pp. 116–130, 1962. </ref> and was introduced by [[Robert Kouyoumjian]] and Prabhakar Pathak in 1974.<ref name="utd"/><ref name="osu-hf">{{cite conference |url= |title=Brief summary of research in high frequency methods at OSU-ESL |last1=Pathak |first1=P. H. |author-link1= |last2= |first2= |author-link2= |date= 2003 |publisher= |book-title= |pages= |location= |conference=Antennas and Propagation Society International Symposium |id= |doi=10.1109/APS.2003.1220345}}</ref>

The uniform theory of diffraction approximates [[Near-field optics|near field]] electromagnetic fields as [[quasi optical]] and uses [[knife-edge diffraction]] to determine diffraction coefficients for each diffracting object-source combination. These coefficients are then used to calculate the field strength and [[phase (waves)|phase]] for each direction away from the diffracting point. These fields are then added to the incident fields and reflected fields to obtain a total solution.
